blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 30 (Spectroscopy-2 NMR), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Name four fields, other than chemistry, in which NMR spectroscopy is used.
blocks.explanation: NMR is used in the polymer industry, in the study of proteins and natural products, in environment monitoring and in the medical field.

book_ref.quote: is a powerful technique which is extensively used in chemistry

blocks.prompt: 2 For what purpose is NMR particularly used in chemistry? Name its two common methods.
blocks.explanation: In chemistry NMR is particularly used to identify organic compounds and determine their structures. The two most common methods are proton (¹H) NMR and carbon-13 (¹³C) NMR.

book_ref.quote: this technique is particularly used for the identification of organic compounds

blocks.prompt: 3 On what property is NMR spectroscopy based? Which atoms usually show NMR signals?
blocks.explanation: NMR spectroscopy is based on the magnetic properties (nuclear spin) of nuclei. Atoms with odd mass numbers, such as ¹H and ¹³C, usually show signals; their nuclei behave like tiny magnets.

book_ref.quote: NMR spectroscopy is based on the magnetic properties (nuclear spin) of nuclei

blocks.prompt: 4 What happens to ¹H nuclei when they are placed in a strong magnetic field?
blocks.explanation: Without a field the nuclei have random orientation and the same energy. In a strong magnetic field they align either with or against the field, giving two spin states: a low energy state and a high energy state.

book_ref.quote: give rise to two spin states i.e., low energy state and high energy state

blocks.prompt: 5 What is spin flipping? How is an NMR spectrum obtained from it?
blocks.explanation: On irradiation with radio waves, nuclei in the low energy state absorb energy and move to the high energy state; this is spin flipping. When they return to their original states they emit energy, which is detected and converted into an NMR spectrum.

book_ref.quote: and move to higher energy state (spin flipping)

blocks.prompt: 6 What is meant by the molecular environment of a nucleus?
blocks.explanation: The exact energy needed to flip a nucleus depends on its position in the compound and on the surrounding atoms; these together are called its molecular environment. Hence NMR can identify hydrogen atoms lying in different environments in one molecule.

book_ref.quote: collectively known as the molecular environment

blocks.prompt: 7 Why do the methyl and hydroxyl hydrogens of methanol absorb different frequencies of radio waves?
blocks.explanation: In CH₃OH three hydrogens are attached to carbon and one to oxygen. The -CH₃ and O-H hydrogens lie in different environments, so they absorb different amounts of energy (different frequencies) for flipping.

book_ref.quote: so they absorb different amount of energy (different frequency of radio waves) for flipping

blocks.prompt: 8 How can nuclei lying in different environments be flipped by radio waves of the same frequency?
blocks.explanation: Nuclei lying in different environments can be flipped by radio waves of the same frequency if the strength of the magnetic field is varied.

book_ref.quote: if the strength of magnetic field is varied

blocks.prompt: 9 Why does ¹²C have no net magnetic field? Do such nuclei always have equal numbers of protons and neutrons?
blocks.explanation: Nuclei with even atomic and even mass numbers have an even number of protons and of neutrons; the protons pair their spins and the neutrons pair theirs, so there is no net magnetic field (e.g. ¹²C). The numbers are not always equal: ¹⁸O has 8 protons and 10 neutrons.

book_ref.quote: The protons pair their spins and the neutrons pair theirs

blocks.prompt: 10 Why are ordinary solvents such as CHCl₃ not used in ¹H NMR?
blocks.explanation: The sample is dissolved in excess solvent. Ordinary solvents contain hydrogen atoms whose strong signals interfere; for example the single proton of CHCl₃ would give a signal intense enough to overlap and mask the weaker signals of the sample.

book_ref.quote: Ordinary solvents contain hydrogen atoms which produce strong signals

blocks.prompt: 11 What are deuterated solvents? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: Deuterated solvents are solvents in which hydrogen (H) is replaced by its isotope deuterium (D). Examples: CDCl₃ (deuterated chloroform) and CD₃OD (deuterated methanol).

book_ref.quote: deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃ (deuterated chloroform) or CD₃OD (deuterated methanol), are used

blocks.prompt: 12 Why is CDCl₃ called a 'silent' solvent in ¹H NMR?
blocks.explanation: Deuterium needs a different frequency of radio waves for flipping, so it does not absorb the radio frequency given to the sample and gives no peak in the ¹H spectrum. Only the sample's signals are seen.

book_ref.quote: This makes the solvent "silent", and only the signals of the sample are observed

blocks.prompt: 13 Define chemical shift. In what unit is it measured?
blocks.explanation: Chemical shift (δ) is the position of a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum relative to the TMS peak (0.0 ppm). It is measured in parts per million (ppm).

book_ref.quote: The position of a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum relative to TMS peak is called the chemical shift

blocks.prompt: 14 What is TMS? What value is assigned to its signal?
blocks.explanation: TMS is tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄, the standard reference compound in NMR. Its signal is assigned 0.0 ppm, and all other proton signals are measured relative to this zero point.

book_ref.quote: Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄ (commonly known as TMS) is used as the standard reference

blocks.prompt: 15 Why does the TMS signal not overlap with most organic proton signals, and why is TMS easy to remove?
blocks.explanation: Because of the low electronegativity of silicon, the TMS protons appear at the extreme right of the spectrum, away from most organic signals. TMS is chemically inert and volatile, so it is easily removed after use.

book_ref.quote: do not overlap with most organic proton signals

blocks.prompt: 16 What does the chemical shift of a proton indicate?
blocks.explanation: Chemical shift indicates the electronic environment of a proton. Protons in different environments have different δ values, while those in the same environment have the same δ value.

book_ref.quote: Chemical shift indicates the electronic environment of a proton

blocks.prompt: 17 What are chemically equivalent protons? Name three compounds in which all protons are equivalent.
blocks.explanation: Protons in chemically identical environments in a molecule are chemically equivalent and show the same chemical shift. All the protons of methane, ethane and benzene (also TMS and propanone) are equivalent, so each gives one peak.

book_ref.quote: All the protons (¹H) found in chemically identical environments within a molecule are chemically equivalent

blocks.prompt: 18 How many proton environments does ethanol (C₂H₅OH) have? Name them.
blocks.explanation: Ethanol has three proton environments: the three -CH₃ protons (one environment), the two -CH₂- protons (a second) and the O-H proton (a third).

book_ref.quote: all the three protons of -CH₃ have same environment, while the two protons of -CH₂- have same environment

blocks.prompt: 19 How does electron density around a proton affect its chemical shift?
blocks.explanation: Protons surrounded by high electron density (alkyl groups) have lower δ values. Protons with low electron density, near electronegative atoms like F, O, N, Cl, appear at higher δ values.

book_ref.quote: The chemical shift of a proton (¹H) is affected by the electron density of its surrounding chemical environment

blocks.prompt: 20 Give reason: in methanol the O-H proton (4.80 ppm) appears at a higher δ than the CH₃ protons (3.35 ppm).
blocks.explanation: The CH₃ protons have a higher electron density around them, so they appear at 3.35 ppm. The O-H proton is next to electronegative oxygen, which lowers its electron density, so it appears at the higher value 4.80 ppm.

book_ref.quote: which appears at 4.80 ppm due to the presence of electronegative oxygen next to it

blocks.prompt: 21 What is the chemical shift range of a ¹H NMR spectrum, and how is Table 30.1 useful?
blocks.explanation: A ¹H NMR spectrum has a δ range of 0 – 12 ppm. Table 30.1 gives the chemical shift ranges of different proton environments, which helps to identify and predict the environment of protons in the spectrum of an unknown compound.

book_ref.quote: This data table is helpful in identifying and predicting the environment of protons

blocks.prompt: 22 Using Table 30.1, give the δ ranges for (i) CH₃–Cl protons and (ii) an aldehyde proton.
blocks.explanation: (i) CH₃–Cl is alkyl next to an electronegative atom: 3.0 – 4.5 ppm. (ii) Aldehyde proton (RCHO): 9.0 – 10.0 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Alkyl next to electronegative atom (halogenoalkanes, alcohols)

blocks.prompt: 23 Distinguish between the δ ranges of alkyl protons in alkanes and aromatic (Ar–H) protons.
blocks.explanation: They differ in electron density and position in the spectrum:

book_ref.quote: Table 30.1 Chemical shifts of some common types of protons

rows: Protons attached to an aromatic ring
Low δ, high electron density (alkyl group)

blocks.prompt: 24 Which three parameters are analysed while interpreting a low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum?
blocks.explanation: (1) The total number of peaks, which gives the number of proton environments; (2) the position of each peak (chemical shift δ), which gives the type of environment; (3) the area under each peak, which gives the relative number of protons.

book_ref.quote: three parameters are carefully analysed; total number of peaks in the spectrum

blocks.prompt: 25 What does the number of peaks in a ¹H NMR spectrum tell us? Give the example of ethanol.
blocks.explanation: Each peak stands for a different chemical environment, so the number of peaks equals the number of proton environments. Ethanol shows three peaks: CH₃, CH₂ and OH protons.

book_ref.quote: Each peak in the spectrum stands for a different chemical environment.

blocks.prompt: 26 Assign the three peaks (5.4, 3.7 and 1.2 ppm) in the low-resolution spectrum of ethanol.
blocks.explanation: 5.4 ppm: OH proton (low electron density environment); 3.7 ppm: –CH₂– next to oxygen; 1.2 ppm: –CH₃ protons.

book_ref.quote: In the spectrum of ethanol (Figure 30.4), the peak at 5.4 ppm represents

blocks.prompt: 27 A compound C₄H₈O₂ gives three peaks with relative areas 4.5 : 3.0 : 4.5. Find the number of protons in each environment.
blocks.explanation: Divide by the smallest area: 4.5/3.0 : 3.0/3.0 : 4.5/3.0 = 1.5 : 1 : 1.5 = 3 : 2 : 3. Sum = 8 = the 8 H of C₄H₈O₂, so the peaks have 3 H, 2 H and 3 H.

book_ref.quote: The area under each peak is proportional to the number of protons giving rise to that peak.

blocks.prompt: 28 How can the total number of hydrogen atoms in a molecule be found from its ¹H NMR spectrum?
blocks.explanation: The peak areas give the number of protons in each environment; adding them gives the total. For ethanol 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 hydrogen atoms.

book_ref.quote: The sum of number of each type of protons gives the total number of protons present in the molecule

blocks.text: 30.4.2 High-Resolution 1H NMR and Splitting of Peaks

blocks.prompt: 29 Why does a peak in a high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum appear as a cluster of sub-peaks?
blocks.explanation: NMR signals are affected not only by nearby electrons but also by protons on adjacent atoms. Each signal is split by the protons on the adjacent carbon atoms, so a peak appears as a cluster of sub-peaks.

book_ref.quote: The NMR signals of protons are not only affected by the nearby electrons

blocks.prompt: 30 State the n+1 rule.
blocks.explanation: A signal usually splits into n + 1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atom(s). Number of sub-peaks = n + 1.

book_ref.quote: A signal usually splits into n+1 sub-peaks

blocks.prompt: 31 Explain the splitting of the -CH₃ and -CH₂- signals in the high-resolution spectrum of ethanol.
blocks.explanation: -CH₃: the adjacent carbon has 2 protons, so 2 + 1 = 3 sub-peaks (triplet). -CH₂-: the adjacent carbon has 3 protons, so 3 + 1 = 4 sub-peaks (quartet).

book_ref.quote: because the number of protons on adjacent carbon is 2 (2+1=3)

blocks.prompt: 32 Give reason: the -OH signal of ethanol is not split.
blocks.explanation: Its hydrogen is bonded to an oxygen atom instead of a carbon atom. -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting and appear as a singlet.

book_ref.quote: The -OH signal is not split because hydrogen is bonded to an oxygen atom

blocks.prompt: 33 Why does ethane give a single unsplit peak although each CH₃ has 3 protons on the adjacent carbon?
blocks.explanation: Chemically equivalent protons do not cause splitting of their neighbouring protons. All six hydrogens of ethane are equivalent, so its peak is a singlet (Figure 30.6).

book_ref.quote: However, the peak does not show splitting because all the hydrogen atoms in ethane are chemically equivalent

blocks.prompt: 34 Name the splitting patterns for n = 0, 1, 2 and 3 with their abbreviations.
blocks.explanation: n = 0: 1 sub-peak, singlet (s); n = 1: 2 sub-peaks, doublet (d); n = 2: 3 sub-peaks, triplet (t); n = 3: 4 sub-peaks, quartet (q).

book_ref.quote: is useful to recognise splitting patterns in high-resolution ¹H NMR spectra

blocks.prompt: 35 Predict the splitting of the CH₃ and CHO signals of ethanal (CH₃CHO).
blocks.explanation: CH₃: the adjacent carbon carries 1 proton, so 1 + 1 = 2 sub-peaks (doublet). CHO: the adjacent carbon carries 3 protons, so 3 + 1 = 4 sub-peaks (quartet).

book_ref.quote: This is due to the splitting of each signal due to the presence of protons (¹H) on adjacent carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 36 Differentiate between low-resolution and high-resolution ¹H NMR spectra.
blocks.explanation: They differ in how much detail each peak shows:

book_ref.quote: This effect can be observed by a high-resolution NMR

rows: Each peak is often a cluster of sub-peaks
Gives number, type and relative number of protons of each environment
Also shows the effect of protons on adjacent carbon atoms
Splitting (n+1 rule) gives the number of neighbouring protons

blocks.text: 30.4.3 Identifying O-H and N-H Protons by D2O Exchange

blocks.prompt: 37 Why do O-H and N-H protons show a wide range of chemical shift? Write the exchange of ethanol with water.
blocks.explanation:
The hydrogens of O-H (alcohols, acids) and N-H (amines, amides) are easily exchangeable, so their singlet shows a wide range of δ.
CH₃–CH₂–O–Hᵃ + Hᵇ–O–Hᵇ ⇌ CH₃–CH₂–O–Hᵇ + Hᵃ–O–Hᵇ

book_ref.quote: The hydrogen atoms in O-H (alcohols or carboxylic acids) and N-H (amines or amides) are easily exchangeable

blocks.prompt: 38 Give reason: in the D₂O shake, only the O-H and N-H peaks disappear, not the C-H peaks.
blocks.explanation: Protons attached to highly electronegative atoms like O or N are easily exchanged with deuterium (R–O–H + D₂O ⇌ R–O–D + HOD), and D gives no ¹H peak. Protons on carbon are not exchanged, so their peaks remain.

book_ref.quote: When D₂O is added to the sample solution, these hydrogens are quickly exchanged with the deuterium (D) atoms

blocks.prompt: 39 Why is a deuterium atom 'invisible' in a ¹H NMR spectrum?
blocks.explanation: Deuterium requires a different energy for spin flipping than ¹H, so it does not show a peak in the ¹H NMR spectrum.

book_ref.quote: As deuterium atom requires different energy for spin flipping as compared to ¹H

blocks.prompt: 40 An amine shows a singlet whose identity is doubtful. How does comparing two spectra confirm that it is an N-H peak?
blocks.explanation: The first spectrum shows all H atoms including N-H. After shaking with a few drops of D₂O the spectrum is recorded again; if that singlet has disappeared, it belonged to the N-H proton.

book_ref.quote: Comparing both spectra confirms the identity of the peak arising due to N-H or O-H

blocks.text: 30.5 Predicting the 1H NMR Spectrum of a Given Molecule

blocks.prompt: 41 List the four steps for predicting the ¹H NMR spectrum of a given molecule.
blocks.explanation: I: identify the different proton environments (= number of peaks). II: estimate δ for each set from Table 30.1. III: predict the splitting of each peak by the n+1 rule. IV: assign integration ratios from the number of H in each environment.

book_ref.quote: This can be done in the following steps:

blocks.prompt: 42 Without a data table, how would you decide which proton set in a molecule has the higher δ?
blocks.explanation: Check the nearest bonds and atoms: protons near electronegative elements have higher δ, while protons in alkyl groups generally have lower δ.

book_ref.quote: The protons near electronegative elements have higher chemical shift (δ)

blocks.prompt: 43 Predict the number of peaks, splitting and area ratio in the ¹H NMR spectrum of bromoethane (CH₃CH₂Br).
blocks.explanation: Two environments, so two peaks. CH₂ (next to Br) at higher δ, 3.0 – 4.5 ppm, quartet (3 + 1); CH₃ at 0.5 – 1.5 ppm, triplet (2 + 1). Area ratio CH₃ : CH₂ = 3 : 2.

book_ref.quote: -CH₂- signal will split into a quartet.

blocks.prompt: 44 Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of methoxymethane (CH₃–O–CH₃).
blocks.explanation: All six protons are equivalent (one environment), so one peak. It is CH₃–O, so δ is 3.0 – 4.5 ppm. The neighbour is O (no protons), so n = 0: a singlet of 6 H.

book_ref.quote: Step II: Estimate the chemical shift (δ) for each set of protons having same chemical environment

blocks.text: 30.6 Determining the Possible Structure of a Molecule from 1H NMR

blocks.prompt: 45 Which pieces of information are combined to deduce a structure from a ¹H NMR spectrum?
blocks.explanation: Number of peaks (number of proton environments), chemical shift of each peak (functional groups), peak areas (number of H in each environment) and splitting (n = sub-peaks – 1, the adjacent protons). These are combined into the structure.

book_ref.quote: It can be done by putting together the following key pieces of information like a puzzle

blocks.prompt: 46 Give reason: the number of peaks in a ¹H NMR spectrum is not the number of protons in the molecule.
blocks.explanation: Equivalent protons give one peak together, so each peak is a set of equivalent protons (an environment). The number of protons in each set comes from the peak areas.

book_ref.quote: The number of peaks equals the number of proton environments (sets of equivalent protons), not the number of protons

blocks.prompt: 47 In Example 30.2, why is the peak at 2.2 ppm (3H) a singlet, and what does it show?
blocks.explanation: A singlet means n = 1 – 1 = 0 neighbouring protons. 2.2 ppm lies in the range for alkyl next to C=O, so this is a CH₃ joined to the C=O carbon (CH₃–C=O).

book_ref.quote: The ¹H NMR spectrum of an ester is given below. Deduce the structure of the ester.

blocks.prompt: 48 In Example 30.2, what is the splitting of the CH₂ signal at 3.9 ppm and why?
blocks.explanation: It is a quartet: the CH₂ next to O has the CH₃ group (3 protons) as neighbour, so 3 + 1 = 4 sub-peaks, i.e. n = 4 – 1 = 3.

book_ref.quote: The CH₂ next to O has three neighbouring protons (the CH₃ group)

blocks.prompt: 49 A compound C₃H₆O₂ gives two singlets, at 2.0 ppm (3H) and 3.7 ppm (3H). Deduce its structure.
blocks.explanation: 2.0 ppm (3H): CH₃ next to C=O; 3.7 ppm (3H): CH₃ next to O. Both singlets, so neither has neighbouring protons. Structure: CH₃–CO–O–CH₃ (methyl ethanoate), C₃H₆O₂.

book_ref.quote: Use peak area to find the actual number of hydrogen atoms for each peak

blocks.prompt: 50 Why is ¹²C NMR inactive while ¹³C is NMR active?
blocks.explanation: ¹²C has even numbers of protons and neutrons (even mass number), so its nucleus has no magnetic property: NMR inactive. ¹³C has an odd number of neutrons, so it possesses magnetic spin and gives NMR spectra.

book_ref.quote: and is, therefore, NMR inactive

blocks.prompt: 51 Which solvent is usually used in ¹³C NMR and where does it give a signal?
blocks.explanation: Deuterated chloroform, CDCl₃, is usually used. Its carbon gives a small signal near 77 ppm (a 1:1:1 triplet centred at 77.16 ppm).

book_ref.quote: The deuterated chloroform (CDCl₃) is usually used as a solvent which produces a small signal

blocks.prompt: 52 Distinguish between the chemical shift ranges and reference of ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR.
blocks.explanation: Both use TMS as the reference but cover different ranges:

book_ref.quote: On the basis of the magnetic properties of carbon-13 isotope

blocks.prompt: 53 What decides the environment of a carbon atom? When are two carbons chemically equivalent?
blocks.explanation: A carbon atom's environment is decided by the types of atoms directly attached to it. Carbons in the same environment are chemically equivalent and show the same chemical shift, e.g. both carbons of ethane.

book_ref.quote: Carbon atoms that are in the same environment are chemically equivalent

blocks.prompt: 54 How many carbon environments are there in 2-methylpropane? Explain.
blocks.explanation: Two. The three methyl carbons are all attached to the same tertiary carbon and have the same environment; the tertiary carbon has a different environment.

book_ref.quote: while the tertiary carbon has different environment than these three carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 55 Using Table 30.3, give the hybridization and δ range of (i) a carbonyl carbon and (ii) a nitrile carbon.
blocks.explanation: (i) Carbonyl carbon (R–CHO, R–CO–R): sp², 190 – 220 ppm. (ii) Nitrile carbon (R–C≡N): sp, 100 – 125 ppm.

book_ref.quote: Table 30.3 Chemical shifts of different carbon environments

blocks.prompt: 56 Differentiate between a carboxyl carbon and a carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR.
blocks.explanation: Both are sp² carbons but appear in different ranges (Table 30.3):

book_ref.quote: The type of environment can be predicted by looking at atoms or bonds around carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 57 Why does ethane show one ¹³C peak while ethanol shows two?
blocks.explanation: In ethane both carbons have the same environment: one peak. In ethanol (CH₃–CH₂–OH) the CH₃ carbon and the CH₂ carbon bonded to O are in different environments: two peaks.

book_ref.quote: ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethane shows only one peak as both the carbon atoms have the same environment

blocks.prompt: 58 Assign the two peaks (18 ppm and about 57 ppm) in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethanol.
blocks.explanation: 18 ppm: the -CH₃ carbon (alkyl range 0 – 50 ppm). About 57 ppm: the -CH₂- carbon bonded to oxygen (C–O range 50 – 70 ppm).

book_ref.quote: it is evident that the peak at 18 ppm is for -CH₃ carbon

blocks.prompt: 59 Write two differences between ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR spectra.
blocks.explanation: The two key differences are in peak area and splitting:

book_ref.quote: There are two key differences between ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR spectra

rows: Peak area shows the number of protons
Peak area usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms
Peaks do not show splitting; they appear as vertical lines

blocks.prompt: 60 Predict the number of ¹³C peaks for (i) butane and (ii) propan-2-ol.
blocks.explanation: (i) Butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃: two end CH₃ carbons equivalent, two middle CH₂ carbons equivalent: 2 peaks. (ii) Propan-2-ol (CH₃)₂CHOH: two CH₃ equivalent, CH–OH different: 2 peaks.

book_ref.quote: the middle -CH₂- carbon has a different environment

blocks.prompt: 61 Predict the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propanone (CH₃COCH₃).
blocks.explanation: Two carbon environments, so two peaks: one for the two equivalent CH₃ carbons (next to carbonyl) and one for the C=O carbon in the carbonyl range 190 – 220 ppm.

book_ref.quote: The ¹³C NMR spectrum is simpler than ¹H NMR

blocks.text: 30.7.3 Determining the Structure of a Molecule from 13C NMR

blocks.prompt: 62 List the steps for working out a structure from a ¹³C NMR spectrum.
blocks.explanation: (1) Count the peaks: number of carbon environments. (2) Look at each peak's position (δ) with Table 30.3 to see what kind of carbon it is. (3) Draw possible structures that fit the molecular formula and the peak count and positions.

book_ref.quote: The ¹³C NMR a spectrum can be used to figure out a molecule's structure

blocks.prompt: 63 Give reason: butan-1-ol cannot be a C₄H₁₀O compound whose ¹³C spectrum shows only 3 peaks.
blocks.explanation: In butan-1-ol all four carbons are in different environments, so it is expected to show 4 peaks. A 3-peak spectrum needs a structure with only 3 carbon environments.

book_ref.quote: It must be a structure with 3 chemical environments

blocks.prompt: 64 Why do the Figure 30.8 shifts (69.0, 30.5, 19.0 ppm) not fit 2-methoxypropane? Which compound do they fit?
blocks.explanation: 2-methoxypropane, CH₃–O–CH(CH₃)₂, would give two carbons bonded to oxygen (about 56 and 72 ppm) and one near 22 ppm. The values fit 2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–OH, which has one C–O carbon and also three carbon environments.

book_ref.quote: which would give two carbons bonded to oxygen (about 56 and 72 ppm) and one near 22 ppm
